Welcome, Our Company & This Orientation

For every member of the patient care team · ≈25–30 minutes

Narration · Welcome

Welcome — and I mean that sincerely. You've joined Praesum Healthcare. What began in 2004 with a single Sunrise Detox location has grown into more than thirty behavioral health centers across the Eastern United States, serving thousands of individuals and families every year — and through every bit of that growth, one idea has stayed constant: the patient comes first. Our centers are built to be comfortable, caring, and competent environments where people can take the medical and psychological steps to a better life, supported by a nationally accredited, ASAM-certified continuum of care. This orientation is for everyone on the care team — nurse practitioners, doctors, nursing, clinical and counseling staff, every patient care team member. And please — reach out to me anytime. Who We Are · Mission & Values
Narration · Comfortable, Caring, Competent

Three words describe the environment we promise every patient: comfortable, caring, and competent. Comfortable, because people heal when they feel safe rather than judged. Caring, because the relationships between members of the team — and between staff and patients — are what people remember most about their stay. And competent, because compassion without clinical excellence isn't enough; our work rests on national accreditation and evidence-based standards. We treat a disease process that manifests in the individual, one that others often don't understand, and we treat the whole person — substance use and the mental-health conditions that so often travel with it. Every site across our family of programs is co-occurring capable.

The Three Pillars — The Spine of Everything That Follows
Teamwork
No one on the care team works in isolation. Decisions about a patient's plan of care belong to the team — never to any one individual. The moment you're tempted to make a change on your own is exactly the moment to loop the team in. You'll see this rule return in every clinical chapter: detox protocols, discharges, psychiatric medication changes — all team decisions.
Communication
Our working rule is simple: if it wasn't communicated and documented, it didn't happen. We bring the team in early, update one another in real time, and close every loop we open. Communication protects patients most at the riskiest moments in care — the transitions and handoffs, which get their own chapter later.
Patient-Centered Care
We treat every patient with dignity and respect, honor their preferences and goals, and make decisions that keep them safe and engaged. Patients tell us the moments that mattered were the human ones: feeling safe enough to talk, being met without judgment, being shown how to change their thinking.

Our Family of Programs
Narration · One Family, One Continuum

Praesum is a family of programs, each meeting patients at a different point in their recovery. Sunrise Detox provides medically supervised withdrawal management with around-the-clock care. Evolve Recovery Center provides residential treatment. Affinity One provides partial hospitalization paired with structured housing. The Counseling Center provides outpatient care, including intensive outpatient and partial-hospitalization programming and medication management. And Beacon Point Recovery Center is part of the family as well. The names matter less than the idea behind them: these aren't separate silos. They're one connected continuum — and a patient can move along it as their needs change, without starting over.

The Programs, At a Glance
Sunrise Detox (SDC)
Medically supervised detoxification with 24/7 care from APNs, nurses, and therapists in a compassionate, non-judgmental setting. Daily counselor sessions, family counseling, group therapy, and case management for legal, FMLA, disability, and primary-care linkage.
Evolve Recovery Center (ERC)
Residential treatment with intensive daily group counseling and individual sessions; psychiatric assessments, NP medication initiation, and MAT.
Affinity One
Partial hospitalization with structured housing; group and individual counseling, family therapy, psychiatric assessments, and MAT. Most clients also engage with TCC services.
The Counseling Center (TCC)
Outpatient, IOP, and PHP across ten New Jersey locations; medication management, MAT, Spravato, and mental-health services including trauma and adolescent groups.
Beacon Point Recovery Center
Part of the Praesum family of recovery programs, extending the continuum of care.
Sunrise footprint
Toms River, NJ (2) · Duluth and Alpharetta, GA · Orlando and Lake Worth, FL · Bentwood, NY · Millbury, MA.

The Meaning of the Continuum
Narration · A Ladder, Not a List

Here's the most important idea to carry out of this chapter — not the details of each level, which you'll learn in depth in Chapter Three, but what the continuum means. Think of our levels of care as a ladder, not a list. A patient doesn't pick a program off a menu; we assess what they need and place them at the least intensive level of care at which they can be safely and effectively treated — intensive enough to be safe, never more restrictive than necessary. As they stabilize, they step down; if they struggle, they can step up. Recovery isn't linear, and the ladder is built for that. Two principles make the ladder work in practice. First, aftercare planning starts on Day 1 — the whole stay points toward the next safe step, not just discharge. Second, every move along the ladder happens with a warm handoff, so no patient falls through the cracks between rungs. That's the difference between a continuum and a collection of programs: the continuum carries the patient.

What the Ladder Means in Practice
Match, don't menu
We place each patient at the least intensive level at which they can be safely and effectively treated — based on assessment, not preference alone or bed availability.
Movement is expected
Patients step down as they stabilize and step up if they struggle. Reassessment is continuous, not a one-time gate (the mechanics are in Chapter Three).
Aftercare starts Day 1
The whole stay points toward the next safe step. Discharge isn't an event at the end — it's a plan from the beginning.
Warm handoff every time
Records, prescriptions, and follow-up are arranged so the receiving team is ready. The continuum carries the patient between rungs.

II.

Your Team & Chain of Command

Nurse practitioner & medical team focus · ≈30 minutes
Listen to this chapter. Checking for recorded narration…
Narration · The Care Team

Let's meet the team — properly, because knowing what each role does is how you route questions to the right person and present clearly at the multidisciplinary team meeting. The nurse practitioner is the medical provider: writing orders, managing medication-assisted treatment, completing the History and Physical and progress notes, and providing clinical leadership within the team. Registered nurses handle triage and assessment, the medication pass, and withdrawal monitoring with tools like CIWA and COWS — nursing will be your closest day-to-day partner. Patient care technicians take vitals, collect drug screens, support admission checks with nursing, and maintain observation. Counselors and therapists complete the clinical assessment, lead daily sessions, write treatment plans, and drive aftercare planning — and, with nursing, they help patients with FMLA and disability paperwork, legal issues, primary-care linkage, and community resources. The Director of Nursing — the DON — is your first point of contact for clinical and medical issues, full stop. The Executive Director leads facility operations. And our medical leadership — the VP of Medical Affairs — provides clinical oversight and is always there for escalation. Every one of these roles is essential, and the magic is in how they work together.

The Roles, In Depth
Who Does What — Day to Day
Nurse Practitioner
Orders and MAT; the H&P and progress notes on the Chapter Four timelines; clinical leadership; daily lab review and sign-off; presenting at the MDT.
Registered Nurse
Triage and the full nursing assessment; the medication pass; CIWA/COWS/HAM-A scoring each assessment; labs; continuous monitoring.
Patient Care Technician
Vitals; urine drug screens; admission consents and checks alongside nursing — including the two-person contraband and skin search; observation rounds.
Counselors / Therapists
Clinical assessment; daily sessions; treatment plans; engagement and aftercare; family counseling and boundary work.
Director of Nursing
First contact for all significant clinical or medical issues. Also backstops the lab loop every morning (Chapter Seven).
Executive Director
Building layout and access; safety procedures and the emergency action plans — medical emergency, lockdown, disaster; scheduling oversight; the process for reporting facility issues with expected follow-up; and the keeper of your completed orientation checklist as the official record.
VP of Medical Affairs
Clinical oversight, scope and protocol questions, and escalation — alongside the facility policy & procedure manual.
Main NP vs. Per Diem NP — Two Lanes, One Team
Main NP
Provides direct patient care four or more days per week. Coordinates detox medications — and any changes to them — with the team. The continuity anchor for every taper in the building.
Per Diem NP
Coordinates with the Main NP, and can order PRN medications and extra doses of medications based on objective data — vitals, withdrawal scores, documented symptoms. What stays out of the per diem lane: rewriting established tapers.
The Chain, Step by Step

Director of Nursing First

ALL significant clinical or medical issues go to the DON first — labs, deterioration, medication concerns, anything that affects patient safety.

Main NP + Treatment Team Clinical decisions

Clinical decisions are made with the Main NP, the DON, and the treatment team in total. The Main NP coordinates the main detox medications.

Executive Director Operations

Operational issues and building logistics — facility access, safety procedures, emergency action plans, reporting facility issues.

Clinical Director Discharge

Discharge-related issues route here — and remember, discharge-date changes also require the Main NP and the full MDT.

Scheduling, presence & coverage NP schedules are created and updated through the Executive Director's process, with availability expectations for main and per diem NPs and required days and times in the building reviewed with the DON. Three practical rules: if you're already on the schedule, you are responsible for finding your own coverage; the backup scheduling contacts are the DON and the Clinical Director; and visibility and accessibility to staff while in the building is an expectation, not a courtesy. Your orientation checklist also covers IT access — Lightning Step (the EHR), EPCS for controlled-substance prescribing, your email, and Microsoft Teams — confirm all four are working before your first solo shift.
The Weekend Rule Weekends need a special rule because the usual day-to-day support may not be on-site. Any concern related to detox medications must reach three people beyond the incoming provider: the DON (all significant clinical issues, first), the Clinical Director (discharge-related issues), and the Main NP (detox-medication continuity and taper decisions). The key word is explicit — flag any detox-medication concern clearly and by name in your handoff, so it cannot be missed when the next provider picks up.

A real weekend handoff — end of taper, e-prescribing down

Telehealth visit. The patient's Ativan taper ended yesterday at 2 mg — an abrupt stepdown the provider flagged as a known protocol limitation worth naming. Today, Ativan 1 mg was given to ease the transition. The note for the next provider: a Suboxone bridge script is needed at the next appointment; Dosespot isn't functional, so the receiving provider may need to write the bridge; and a weekend flag went to the DON, the Clinical Director, and the Main APN — detox-med end-point concern plus the e-prescribing gap. Nursing was asked to monitor for rebound withdrawal and anxiety overnight, using comfort meds per protocol.

Notice the anatomy: the concern is named explicitly, the three weekend contacts are flagged by role, the administrative obstacle is documented, and nursing gets a concrete monitoring plan. That's the weekend rule working.

Two rules to remember (1) Early discharges, or any change to a discharge date, require the Main NP and the full multidisciplinary team — even the Main NP cannot make that change alone, and the team confirms the patient is stable and ready. (2) Any question about clinical practice, a protocol, or your scope goes to the DON, the VP of Medical Affairs, or the facility policy & procedure manual. When in doubt, ask — escalation is a strength, not a weakness.

III.

The ASAM Levels of Care — Applying the Continuum

For the whole team · clinical framework · ≈35–40 minutes
Listen to this chapter. Checking for recorded narration…
Narration · Why ASAM, and Which Edition

In Chapter One we talked about the continuum as a ladder. This chapter is how we actually climb it. The framework we use is The ASAM Criteria — the American Society of Addiction Medicine's standards, and the nation's most comprehensive guideline set for three decisions: placement, continued stay, and transfer or discharge. The current standard is the Fourth Edition, published in December 2023, and it's the version states and payers are adopting across 2025 and 2026 — so it's the edition we document to. A quick note on what's new, because some of you trained on the Third Edition: the Fourth Edition integrates medically managed care into the main continuum, adds a new long-term remission monitoring level, and — most importantly for assessment — replaces the old "readiness to change" dimension with a new person-centered dimension. Let's build it from the ground up: the three core components, the six dimensions, the levels themselves, and then how all of that lands in your documentation and your daily role.

How the Criteria Work · Three Core Components
Narration · Assessment → Admission Criteria → Levels

The ASAM Criteria have three core components that work in tandem. First, when a patient enters treatment, you complete a Level of Care Assessment that identifies their clinical needs across the dimensions. Second, you apply those findings to the Dimensional Admission Criteria, which translate the assessment into a recommended level of care — specifically, the least intensive but safe level for that patient. Third, the Criteria define standards for each level of care across the continuum: the setting, the staffing, the service intensity, and the core elements you'll find at each rung. And then there's the piece that never stops: as the patient moves through treatment, you reassess. The transition and continued service criteria tell you whether the patient is ready to step down to a less intensive level, needs to step up to a more intensive one, or should continue where they are. Assessment isn't a gate you pass once at the door — it's a loop you run for the whole stay.

Level of Care Assessment Identify needs

On entry, assess the patient's clinical needs across the six dimensions — intoxication and withdrawal, biomedical, psychiatric/cognitive, substance-use risks, recovery environment, and person-centered factors.

Dimensional Admission Criteria Recommend a level

Apply the assessment to the admission criteria to determine the recommended level of care — the least intensive level at which the patient can be safely and effectively treated.

Levels of Care Standards Deliver

Each level defines its setting, staffing, and service intensity. Match the patient to the level whose standards meet their needs.

Transition & Continued Service Reassess

Reassess regularly: step down, step up, or continue. This is the engine of the continuum — recovery isn't linear, so placement isn't permanent.

The Six Dimensions (Fourth Edition)
Narration · What's New, and How They Drive Placement

Every assessment is built on six dimensions — a biopsychosocial picture of the patient. Dimension One is intoxication, withdrawal, and addiction medications. Dimension Two is biomedical conditions and complications. Dimension Three is psychiatric and cognitive conditions. Dimension Four is substance-use-related risks. Dimension Five is recovery environment interactions. And Dimension Six — new in the Fourth Edition — is person-centered considerations: barriers to care including the social determinants of health, the patient's own preferences, and the need for motivational enhancement. Here's the change that matters most: the old Third-Edition Dimension Four, "readiness to change," no longer stands alone in driving the level of care. Instead, readiness is woven through the other dimensions and shapes the services delivered at any level. And the way the dimensions combine is specific — Dimensions One through Five generate the level-of-care recommendation, while Dimension Six is applied through shared decision-making with the patient to land on the level they're actually willing and able to engage in. The Fourth Edition also defines subdimensions under each dimension; the ones highlighted in the assessment drive the recommendation and immediate needs, but all of them inform the treatment plan.

DimensionWhat You Assess · How It's Used
1Intoxication, withdrawal & addiction medications — drives LOC recommendation
2Biomedical conditions & complications — drives LOC recommendation
3Psychiatric & cognitive conditions — drives LOC recommendation
4Substance use–related risks — drives LOC recommendation
5Recovery environment interactions — drives LOC recommendation
6Person-centered considerations (NEW) — SDOH barriers, preferences, motivation; applied via shared decision-making for the level the patient will engage in

Readiness to change didn't disappear — it moved

If you trained on the Third Edition, you knew "readiness to change" as Dimension Four. In the Fourth Edition it no longer independently sets the level of care. Instead, it informs the clinical judgment of risk within the other dimensions and shapes which services you deliver at whatever level the patient is in — and it lives most visibly now inside Dimension Six's motivational-enhancement focus.

Practical upshot: don't place someone in a higher level "because they're not ready." Place by Dimensions 1–5, then use Dimension 6 and motivational work to meet them where they are.

The Continuum · Four Broad Levels, Many Gradations
Narration · Reading the Numbers

Now the ladder itself. The continuum has four broad levels, one through four, and within them decimal numbers express finer gradations of intensity and the type of care provided. Level One is outpatient. Level Two is intensive outpatient and partial hospitalization. Level Three is residential and inpatient care of increasing intensity. Level Four is medically managed intensive inpatient — the most acute. A few Fourth-Edition specifics worth knowing. There's a brand-new Level One-point-zero, long-term remission monitoring, for patients in sustained recovery — recovery-management check-ups and rapid re-engagement if they slip, which is the chronic-care model in action. Medically managed care is now built into the main continuum rather than sitting off to the side. You'll also see enhanced designations: "BIO," as in three-point-seven BIO, for enhanced biomedical capability, and "COE," co-occurring enhanced, for levels staffed to treat co-occurring mental-health conditions — and a Level Four Psychiatric for the most acute co-occurring needs. And the admission criteria can now recommend a recovery residence alongside an outpatient level. Here's how our own programs map onto that ladder.

ASAM LevelWhat It Is · Where It Lives Here
1.0Long-term remission monitoring (NEW) — recovery check-ups, rapid re-engagement
1.5Outpatient therapy (TCC)
2.1Intensive outpatient — 9–19 h/week (TCC)
2.5Partial hospitalization — ≥ 20 h/week (Affinity One, with structured housing)
2.7Medically managed intensive outpatient
3.1Low-intensity residential (9–19 h/week of services)
3.5High-intensity residential (Evolve Recovery Center)
3.7 / 3.7 BIOMedically managed residential; BIO = enhanced biomedical capability
4Medically managed intensive inpatient — withdrawal management (Sunrise Detox)
COE levels · 4 PsychiatricCo-occurring enhanced staffing (e.g., 2.5 COE, 3.5 COE); 4 Psychiatric for acute co-occurring

Applying It · Placement, SUD Treatment & Your Role
Narration · From Framework to Practice

So how does all this show up in your daily work? Three ways. First, placement: you use the dimensional admission criteria to match the patient to the least intensive safe level, and you reassess against the continued-service criteria so the patient steps down as they stabilize. Second, substance-use treatment itself: the level sets the container, but the dimensions shape what happens inside it — Dimension One drives the withdrawal protocols you'll meet in Chapter Five, Dimension Three drives the psychiatric care in Chapter Six, and medication for addiction is integrated right into the continuum rather than bolted on. Third — and this is where a lot of good clinical work gets lost — documentation. The Criteria decide the level of care; your records decide whether that level survives a payer's review. Every dimension documented, with risk ratings and no blanks, is what justifies the level you placed the patient in, supports Utilization Review's authorization, and defends continued stay. We also have tools that support this: ASAM CONTINUUM is a full electronic assessment with computerized decision support, Co-Triage gives a quick provisional referral level, and the ASAM Criteria Navigator supports utilization review and management. Whatever tool you use, the discipline is the same: assess all six dimensions, place at the least intensive safe level, reassess on a schedule, and document to the level you're delivering and billing.

The Three Applications
Placement
Apply the Dimensional Admission Criteria → least intensive safe level. Reassess against continued-service criteria → step down, step up, or continue. Use Dimension 6 and shared decision-making for the level the patient will actually engage in.
SUD treatment
The level is the container; the dimensions shape the care inside it. Dimension 1 → withdrawal protocols (Chapter Five). Dimension 3 → psychiatric care (Chapter Six). Medication for addiction is integrated across the continuum, not separate.
Documentation & your role
Document every dimension with risk ratings and no blanks — it justifies the level placed, supports UR authorization, and defends continued stay. The Criteria decide the level; your records decide whether it survives review.

IV.

Admission, Monitoring & Documentation

Nurse practitioner & medical team focus · ≈30–35 minutes
Listen to this chapter. Checking for recorded narration…
Narration · The First Four Hours

The admission sets up everything that follows, and the first four hours have a rhythm. Two rules sit above all of it: verify two patient identifiers before any clinical task, and check the release of information before any call — no ROI, no call. On arrival, the RN triages, capturing substances, amount, duration, last use, medical and seizure history, and every current medication, including every prescription. After the RN clears the patient, the technician completes consents, vitals, the urine drug screen, a pregnancy test for every female-born patient, and the contraband and skin search together with the nurse — that's a two-person check, every time. The full nursing assessment is completed within four hours, and any exception — a medical send-out, intoxication — is documented; no exception means no excuse. Right after come the initial treatment plan and the admission blood draws — a CMP, RPR, QuantiFERON, and CBC. The same visit includes the PHQ-9, GAD-7, and C-SSRS, because those scores drive the psychiatric consult decisions in Chapter Six. And medication reconciliation starts immediately: verify home psychiatric and medical medications for restart, with the PDMP for anything controlled — and never delay waiting on family or pill bottles. Verify in parallel, never serially.

The First Four Hours, In Sequence

Triage RN · on arrival

Substances, amount, duration, last use, medical and seizure history, and every current medication — capture each prescription med too. This is the data that drives the right protocol later.

Consents, vitals, UDS, pregnancy test, contraband & skin search Tech, with nurse

After the RN clears the patient. The skin and contraband search is a two-person check with nursing. Pregnancy test for every female-born patient.

Complete the nursing assessment RN · within 4 h

Document any exception — medical send-out, intoxication. No exception = no excuse.

Initial treatment plan & admission blood draws RN

Labs: CMP, RPR, QuantiFERON, CBC — drawn in the correct CLSI order of draw.

Mental-health screen RN / clinician

PHQ-9, GAD-7, and C-SSRS — these scores drive the psychiatric consult decisions you'll learn in Chapter Six.

Medication reconciliation RN / pharmacist · immediately

Verify home psych and medical meds for restart; PDMP for anything controlled. No delay waiting for family — verify in parallel.

Before the first session Counselor

Call the emergency contact (after checking the ROI), review the UA/BAC, verify consents and ROIs, and confirm the ASAM assessment is done.

Pause and picture it. A patient arrives at 2 a.m., frightened and sick. In four hours, a stranger becomes a known patient with a plan: identified, screened, lab-drawn, risk-rated, and reconciled — without a single step skipped, and without waiting on a pill bottle that may never arrive. That choreography is patient-centered care in its most practical form.
The First Four Hours · Admission & Triage
Narration · A Choreographed Start

The admission is choreographed, and the order matters. Before any clinical task, two patient identifiers are confirmed — a Joint Commission National Patient Safety Goal that prevents wrong-patient errors. The registered nurse triages first, capturing the substances used including any prescription medication, the amount, the length of use, the last use, the full medical and surgical history, the seizure history, and all current home medications. After the RN clears the patient to the level of care, the behavioral health technician obtains consents, vital signs, a urine drug screen, a pregnancy test for every female-born patient, and conducts the contraband search and skin assessment with a nurse — a two-person check. The complete nursing assessment is documented within four hours of arrival; the only acceptable exceptions, like a medical send-out or intoxication that precludes interview, must themselves be documented. Then comes the initial treatment plan, the admission blood draws, the baseline mental-health screens, and — immediately — medication reconciliation, so home medications can be restarted without delay. Counseling prepares in parallel: calling the emergency contact before meeting the client, reviewing labs so every substance lands in the clinical assessment, confirming consents and releases of information, and confirming the ASAM is complete.

StepWho & What
IdentifyConfirm two patient identifiers before any clinical task (Joint Commission NPSG)
TriageRN: substances, amount, length of use, last use, medical/surgical & seizure history, current meds
Intake checksBHT with nurse: consents, vitals, UDS, pregnancy test (female-born), two-person contraband & skin assessment
AssessFull nursing assessment documented within 4 hours; exceptions documented
Plan & labsInitial treatment plan; admission bloods (CMP, RPR, QuantiFERON-TB Gold, CBC)
ScreenPHQ-9, GAD-7, C-SSRS during the nursing assessment (drives §27 consults)
ReconcileMedication reconciliation immediately — restart home meds without delay (verify in parallel, never serially)
Mental-Health Screening · Thresholds That Trigger Action
Narration · Three Validated Screens

Three validated screens run at intake and throughout the stay, and each carries action thresholds you must know. The PHQ-9 scores depression zero to twenty-seven: ten to fourteen is moderate and indicates a psychiatric consult after the care team discusses the specific positive scores; fifteen to nineteen requires consultation; twenty and above is urgent. And the single most important rule on the PHQ-9 is item nine — any positive endorsement of thoughts of being better off dead or of self-harm, regardless of total score, triggers immediate completion of the C-SSRS, immediate provider notification, and continuous safety monitoring. The C-SSRS stratifies suicide risk in five levels, with escalating responses you'll see in the table. The GAD-7 scores anxiety zero to twenty-one, with fifteen and above indicating a consult. If the PHQ-9 is above nine, the clinician completes a safety plan and alerts the Patient Care Team. These numbers are not paperwork — they are the difference between catching risk and missing it.

Screen & ScoreRequired Action
PHQ-9 5–9Mild — monitor, supportive care, consider counseling referral
PHQ-9 10–14Moderate — consult; verify home antidepressant restart
PHQ-9 15–19Moderately severe — consult required
PHQ-9 20–27Severe — URGENT consult
PHQ-9 item 9 positiveAny score → complete C-SSRS, notify provider, continuous monitoring + safety plan
C-SSRS L3Method, no plan → urgent consult + Q15 monitoring
C-SSRS L4Some intent → 1:1 sitter, means restriction, transfer eval
C-SSRS L5Plan & intent → immediate consult, continuous 1:1, transfer
GAD-7 15–21Severe — psychiatric consult indicated
The Biopsychosocial Assessment
Narration · The Whole Person

The biopsychosocial assessment is the comprehensive intake completed for every admission — the structured way we see the whole person, not just the substance. It captures basic information and preferred pronouns and language; household composition and whether home is a safe place; the precipitating event in the patient's own words; substance-use history substance by substance; treatment history; family and developmental history; social, spiritual, and cultural identification; employment and education; legal status; military service; medical history and medications; nutrition; emotional and behavioral conditions; and a thorough risk-and-safety section covering trauma, self-harm, suicidal and homicidal ideation, and protective factors. Two principles run through it. First, it's trauma-informed: we lead sensitive questions with "If you feel comfortable…", we ask consent, and we honor a patient's choice not to answer. Second, it's person-centered, which maps directly onto ASAM Dimension Six. The assessment closes with the recommended ASAM level of care, the current relapse risk for both mental health and substance use, the stage of change, and an individualized problem list — and Problem One on every treatment plan is always the substance use disorder.

The BPS, At a Glance — What It Captures
Identity & home
Pronouns, language, sexual orientation (asked with consent); household composition and safety; housing stability.
The story
Precipitating event in the patient's own words; substance-by-substance history; treatment history; longest period of sobriety; what kept them motivated.
Background
Family and developmental history; social, spiritual, and cultural identification; employment, education, legal status, and military service.
Medical & behavioral
Medical history, PCP, medications, allergies, disabilities, nutrition (3+ flags → referral); emotional/behavioral conditions.
Risk & safety
Trauma (past/present/family), self-harm, SI/HI with C-SSRS, and a protective-factors checklist — risk addressed in the treatment and discharge plans.
Closing
Recommended ASAM level (no blanks), relapse risk (MH + SUD), stage of change, and an individualized problem list — Problem 1 is always Substance Use Disorder.
Documentation · DAP Notes & Standards
Narration · Data, Assessment, Plan

We document in the DAP format — Data, Assessment, Plan — and every note carries a patient quote. Data is information, not interpretation: what the patient reported, their withdrawal symptoms and CIWA or COWS score, cravings, sleep, appetite, group attendance, and any emergency-contact call. Assessment applies your clinical judgment to that data — how the patient is progressing, their stage of change, their relapse risk — and every conclusion must be clearly supported by the data above it. Plan is where treatment goes next: the next session, homework, referrals, and any changes to the treatment plan. The timelines are firm and auditable: in detox the History and Physical is completed within twenty-four hours with daily progress notes; in residential, within thirty-six to forty-eight hours with notes every two to three days. And the discipline that protects everyone is this — documentation must satisfy clinical, licensing, payer, and CMS requirements and must support the level of care billed, with risk-rated findings across all six ASAM dimensions and no blanks. When you use the Co-Pilot assistant, it's configured to incorporate the ASAM dimensions and to never add clinical information that wasn't provided.

D — Data Facts only

Client report, withdrawal symptoms with CIWA/COWS score, cravings, sleep, appetite, group attendance, EC contact. Direct quotes where appropriate — no interpretation here.

A — Assessment Judgment

How the patient is progressing, stage of change, relapse risk — every conclusion supported by the Data section. ASAM dimensions rated with reasoning.

P — Plan Next steps

Next session date/time, homework, referrals, consultations, and any treatment-plan changes based on progress.

Every note Quote

Every note gets a patient quote — it preserves the patient's voice and supports motivational-interviewing fidelity.

Documentation timelines (auditable) Detox: H&P within 24 hours of admission; progress notes daily. Residential: H&P within 36–48 hours; progress notes every 2–3 days. Every clinical assessment enters the ASAM level with no blanks, supported by risk-rated findings across Dimensions 1–5 and Dimension 6. Non-compliant documentation is subject to audit and can cause claim denial — but more importantly, the chart is how the next clinician knows what you knew.
Admission Labs & Point-of-Care Testing
What's Drawn, and the Order of Draw
Every admission
Urine drug screen with specimen-validity testing (specific gravity, creatinine, pH) sent to Quest for confirmation; plus CMP, RPR, QuantiFERON-TB Gold, and CBC.
Case-specific
Lithium level, prolactin, valproic acid level — and any test the provider adds on clinical indication.
Order of draw (CLSI GP41)
Gold-top SST → green-top → lavender-top. The SST tube stands upright 10–15 minutes before centrifugation; QuantiFERON is packaged separately.
Result review
The DON reviews unassigned reports each morning; the NP reviews and signs results daily and orders treatment for any abnormal value.
POC quality control
Under a CLIA Certificate of Waiver: HemoCue glucose controls on each diabetic admission and daily; UDS/pregnancy controls per shipment and lot; breathalyzer calibrated daily; specimen fridge 2–8 °C logged every shift.
Confidentiality · The Rules You Work Under
HIPAA · 42 CFR Part 2 · CLIA Protected health information is accessed only on a minimum-necessary basis; patient conversations happen only in private areas; systems use unique logins with no password sharing; workstations lock when unattended and printed PHI is shredded. 42 CFR Part 2 gives substance-use-disorder records heightened protection — the 2024 Final Rule aligned it with HIPAA for treatment, payment, and operations while preserving protections against use in legal proceedings. A signed Release of Information is required for any disclosure outside the treatment team, and is documented in the chart. The rule of thumb you'll use daily: no ROI, no call.

Two Standards Every Note Must Meet
Every note tells the story
Use DAP format — Data, Assessment, Plan — and include a brief patient quote, so the note reflects the patient's own words and engagement rather than boilerplate. Support it with risk-rated findings across ASAM Dimensions 1–6, with no blanks.
Meet every standard

Why it mattersThorough ASAM-dimension documentation is what Utilization Review uses to secure the authorization that matches the patient's clinical need. When you document well, you're directly protecting the patient's access to the right level of care — good notes protect the patient, the team, and the organization.

V.

Medications & Withdrawal Protocols

Nurse practitioner & medical team focus · ≈40–45 minutes
Listen to this chapter. Checking for recorded narration…
Narration · The One Rule Above All

This is the clinical heart of the program, and it's the longest chapter for a reason. Before anything else, the single most important rule: no medication is ever given without an active provider order. When in doubt, call the provider — and always practice within your professional scope. Four principles anchor everything you'll do here. First, hold detox protocols: established medications and tapers aren't altered unless clinically necessary, and when you do make a change, document why. Second, less is more: limit new orders, and reach for comfort medications before adding scheduled medications. Third, loop in the team — discuss any plan-of-care change with the treatment team before acting; don't change protocols on your own. And fourth, escalate on weekends: detox-medication concerns go to the DON and the Main NP, flagged explicitly. These four principles protect the patient, protect continuity across providers, and protect you. Everything in this chapter reflects current ASAM, SAMHSA, and FDA evidence-based guidelines.

No orderNo med. No exceptions. When in doubt, call the provider.
Less is moreComfort meds before new scheduled orders.
HoldDon't alter established tapers unless clinically necessary — and document why.
EscalateWeekend detox-med concerns → DON + Main NP, flagged explicitly.
Comfort Meds First — The Symptom-Relief Toolkit

All require an active order. The discipline here is what protects the detox protocol underneath.

The PRN Toolkit · Comfort Medications in Depth
Narration · Comfort First, and Know Each Agent

Comfort medications are the backbone of a humane detox, and "less is more" means reaching for symptom relief before adding scheduled medications. But comfort-first only works if you know each agent — its mechanism, what it treats, and what makes it unsafe for a given patient. Every PRN here requires an active provider order. A few that deserve special attention: clonidine, an alpha-2 agonist, treats hypertension, tremor, sweating, and generalized withdrawal — but verify blood pressure before each dose, because it is also an antihypertensive. Hydroxyzine helps anxiety and nausea but is avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Trazodone and mirtazapine both help sleep but are never combined with an MAOI, because of serotonin syndrome. And loperamide for diarrhea carries a quiet risk — at high doses it has opioid-like effects, so we do mouth checks to prevent diversion. The table that follows is your quick reference; learn the contraindications, because that's where patient safety lives.

PRN · ClassTreats · Key Cautions
Clonidine (α2-agonist)HTN, tremor, sweating, generalized withdrawal — verify BP before each dose; hold for hypotension
Hydroxyzine (antihistamine)Anxiety, nausea — avoid in pregnancy/breastfeeding; SE dry mouth, constipation, dizziness
Propranolol (β-blocker)Tachycardia, anxiety, tremor — caution in diabetes, COPD/asthma, bradycardia
Methocarbamol / RobaxinMuscle spasm, restless legs — caution renal/hepatic impairment, pregnancy
Trazodone (SARI)Insomnia — never with an MAOI (serotonin syndrome)
Quetiapine low-doseInsomnia — SE somnolence, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness
Mirtazapine / RemeronInsomnia — caution renal/hepatic, pregnancy; never with an MAOI
MelatoninInsomnia — caution with anticoagulants, anticonvulsants, antihypertensives, diabetes
Ondansetron / Zofran (5-HT3)Nausea/emesis — caution in severe hepatic impairment, pregnancy
Promethazine / PhenerganSevere nausea/emesis — caution in seizure history and pregnancy; sedating
Maalox / Milk of MagnesiaReflux / constipation — caution with electrolyte imbalance, renal impairment

Ibuprofen (NSAID)Pain, headache, fever — avoid with anticoagulants, pregnancy; caution GI/renal/hepatic
Acetaminophen / TylenolPain, fever — contraindicated in hepatic impairment

Detox Pharmacology · Why Each First-Line Agent
Narration · The Drugs Behind the Protocols

Understanding why we choose each agent makes the protocols make sense. For alcohol, Librium — chlordiazepoxide — is first-line: a long-acting benzodiazepine with active metabolites and a twenty-four to forty-eight-hour half-life, which produces a smooth, partly self-tapering course. When the liver is impaired, we switch to Ativan — lorazepam — because it's cleared by conjugation only, with no active metabolites, so its clearance is preserved in cirrhosis. For opioids, buprenorphine is a long-acting partial agonist that stabilizes the mu receptor, prevents withdrawal, and blocks other opioids, with a low overdose risk and a roughly thirty-eight-hour half-life; the naloxone in Suboxone isn't absorbed sublingually but deters injection. Subutex, the monoproduct, is reserved for pregnancy and methadone-to-buprenorphine transitions, where it lowers precipitated-withdrawal risk. Methadone is a full agonist with no precipitated-withdrawal risk at induction, but it prolongs the QT interval — so a baseline EKG matters — and it's why seizure-history patients on methadone get Keppra instead of phenobarbital, since phenobarbital induces the CYP enzymes that clear methadone. For benzodiazepines, Valium — diazepam — is first-line precisely because its long half-life and active metabolites make it self-tapering, and it is never stopped abruptly.

AgentClass · Pharmacology · Use
Librium (chlordiazepoxide)Long-acting benzo; active metabolites; t½ 24–48 h — first-line alcohol; caution hepatic/renal, pregnancy, elderly
Ativan (lorazepam)Short-acting benzo; conjugated only, no active metabolites; t½ 12–18 h — preferred when hepatic function impaired
Suboxone (bup–naloxone)Partial agonist + antagonist; t½ ~38 h; naloxone deters IV/IN misuse — first-line opioid
Subutex (buprenorphine)Partial agonist monoproduct — pregnancy and methadone-to-bup transitions (lower precipitated-withdrawal risk)
MethadoneFull agonist, Schedule II; no precipitated withdrawal at induction; prolongs QT — baseline EKG; Keppra (not phenobarbital) for seizure history
Valium (diazepam)Long-acting benzo; t½ ~48 h + active metabolites → self-tapering — first-line benzo detox; never stop abruptly
Emergency medications — act, then transfer Naloxone (Narcan): for suspected opioid overdose, reverses respiratory depression; precipitates acute withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients. Because its duration (≈30–90 min) is shorter than most opioids, every patient who receives it is transferred to the ED for re-sedation risk; watch for rare non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Epinephrine (Epi-Pen): for anaphylaxis, give epinephrine first — antihistamines and steroids are second-line and don't reverse airway compromise — then transfer with continuous monitoring.

Symptom-triggered, not fixed-dose

Praesum titrates benzodiazepines to the CIWA-Ar rather than a fixed schedule. The 2020 ASAM alcohol-withdrawal guideline supports this: symptom-triggered therapy reduces total benzodiazepine exposure, shortens length of stay, and lowers over-sedation while still preventing seizures and delirium tremens. The scores aren't a formality — they're the dosing instrument.

Score the patient, treat the score, document the score. The CIWA-Ar titrates treatment; it does not diagnose withdrawal.

Monitoring Tools — Titrate Treatment, Don't Diagnose
ToolScore Bands & Action
COWS (opioid)5–12 mild · 13–24 moderate · 25–36 moderately severe · >36 severe. Induce buprenorphine at COWS ≥ 16 — our conservative threshold to minimize precipitated withdrawal.
CIWA-Ar (alcohol)<8 mild · 8–15 moderate · >15 severe — assess and monitor for delirium tremens. CIWA-B is the benzodiazepine parallel.
HAM-A (anxiety)0–7 none · 8–17 mild · 18–24 mild-moderate · 25–30 moderate-severe · >30 severe. Used for moderate-to-severe anxiety, opioid patients awaiting induction, and general anxiety needing extra medication.
EvidenceSymptom-triggered, benzodiazepine-based therapy guided by the CIWA-Ar reduces total benzodiazepine exposure and length of stay compared with fixed-dose protocols (ASAM, 2020). The tools exist to titrate treatment to the patient in front of you — not to make a diagnosis.
Narration · Protocols Are Driven by Duration of Use

Here are the core withdrawal protocols, and the key is that they're driven by how long the patient has been using. For alcohol, Librium is first-line for patients under fifty-five, and Ativan for those fifty-five and older or with hepatic impairment — Ativan is cleared by conjugation only, with no active metabolites, so its clearance is preserved when liver function is reduced. For opiates, Suboxone is first-line, or Subutex, the monoproduct, if the patient is pregnant or coming off methadone. For benzodiazepines, a Valium taper — and never, ever stopped abruptly, because Valium's long half-life and active metabolites give it a self-tapering profile. For stimulants, there is no FDA-approved detox protocol: stabilize, provide supportive care, and watch for stimulant-induced psychosis and the post-binge crash. And xylazine modifies the opiate protocol, because alpha-2 rebound is the danger. Let's walk each one in detail.

The Detox Agents, In Brief
Long-acting benzo

Librium (chlordiazepoxide)

First-line for alcohol <55. Half-life 24–48 h with active metabolites.

Caution: hepatic/renal impairment, pregnancy, elderly.
Short-acting benzo

Ativan (lorazepam)

Preferred in hepatic impairment — conjugated, no active metabolites, clearance preserved. Half-life 12–18 h.

Caution: hepatic/renal, pregnancy, elderly.
Long-acting benzo

Valium (diazepam)

First-line for benzo withdrawal. ~48 h half-life with active metabolites → self-tapering profile.

Never discontinue abruptly in dependent patients.
Partial agonist

Suboxone / Subutex

Opiate first-line. Subutex (monoproduct) if pregnant or off methadone — minimizes precipitated withdrawal and fetal naloxone exposure.

Induce at COWS ≥ 16.
Seizure precautions — every patient with a lifetime seizure history Default: phenobarbital 32.4 mg PO TID × 4 days for seizure-history patients detoxing from alcohol, opiates (non-methadone), benzodiazepines, or stimulants. Substitute Keppra (levetiracetam) 500 mg PO TID × stay for methadone protocols, xylazine, or phenobarbital allergy — because phenobarbital is a potent CYP3A4 inducer that accelerates methadone clearance and can precipitate withdrawal. So the phenobarbital-versus-Keppra choice is really a CYP3A4 question. Hold phenobarbital for lethargy or nystagmus. Evidence: adjunct phenobarbital reduced ICU length of stay and the need for additional sedatives without increasing intubation in a 2023 meta-analysis.
Emergencies — act, then transfer Narcan (naloxone): suspected opioid overdose → give. It acts thirty to ninety minutes — shorter than most opioids — so transfer to the ED every time, because of re-sedation risk. Epi-Pen (epinephrine): anaphylaxis → give epinephrine first, before anything else; antihistamines and steroids are second-line. Transfer to the ED. High-risk Q15 monitoring × 24 h applies to the methadone protocol, xylazine within four hours of last use, and severe withdrawal.

VI.

Restarting Meds & Psychiatric Care

Nurse practitioner & medical team focus · ≈35–40 minutes
Listen to this chapter. Checking for recorded narration…
Narration · Continuity Is a Safety Priority

Continuity of medication is a core safety priority, and it's one of the most common places early care goes wrong. When a patient arrives, restarting their clinically necessary home medications is never delayed while we wait on lab results, family contact, or someone bringing in pill bottles. The trick is to verify in parallel, never serially: you start with the patient's self-reported list — name, strength, frequency, and last dose — while PDMP, pharmacy, and provider verification all proceed at the same time. Anticonvulsants, antihypertensives, insulin, and anticoagulants are the ones you do not want interrupted; they restart at provider order. And the reason we restart promptly isn't just comfort — the discontinuation of antidepressants and other agents produces symptoms that get mistaken for relapse or new psychiatric illness, which can send the whole plan of care in the wrong direction. So: restart what's safe, restart it early, and monitor.

The Restart Framework
Narration · Dose by Time Since Last Dose

The restart dose follows a simple principle — the longer the gap since the last dose, the more conservatively you re-introduce, because tolerance fades over time. This framework is the standard across SSRIs, SNRIs, atypical antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, stimulants, and anxiolytics. Under two weeks, resume the last effective dose. Two to four weeks, restart at about fifty percent and titrate to target over one to two weeks. Four to six weeks, use the standard initial dose and titrate per the labeled schedule over two to four weeks. And beyond six weeks, treat it as a brand-new start with full titration. Hold those numbers in mind — and then hold two exceptions even more firmly, because the FDA mandates them regardless of the gap.

Time Since Last DoseRestart Approach
Under 2 weeksResume the last effective dose
2–4 weeks~50% of last effective dose; titrate to target over 1–2 weeks
4–6 weeksStandard initial dose; titrate per labeled schedule over 2–4 weeks
Over 6 weeksFull re-initiation — treat as a new start
Two FDA-mandated re-titrations — non-negotiable, regardless of the gap Clozapine: more than 48 hours since the last dose → must re-titrate from 12.5 mg regardless of the prior dose — risk of cardiac collapse. Requires a provider order plus Clozapine REMS ANC monitoring; per our guidance we rarely have these patients, so call the DON and the VP of Medical Affairs. Lamotrigine: more than 5 days → must re-titrate from 25 mg/day — Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis risk with rapid restart. These two override the time-since-dose table entirely.
The Verification Workflow · Restart Without Delay
Narration · Six Steps, Run in Parallel

Restarting home medications safely starts with a disciplined verification workflow — and the cardinal rule is that verification and provider notification proceed in parallel, never in series, so no clinically necessary medication waits. Six steps: start with the patient's self-reported list — name, strength, frequency, last dose, prescriber, and pharmacy. Check the state Prescription Drug Monitoring Program for every controlled substance; per the 2022 CDC guideline, PDMP review belongs at every admission. Check the Lightning Step prescription module for prior-fill history inside our system. Call the home pharmacy to confirm the medication, strength, last fill, and prescriber, documenting the pharmacist's name and the time. Call the prescriber's office when pharmacy verification is incomplete or clinical input is needed. And communicate the verified list to the admitting provider, who issues the orders — because no medication is administered without an active order. Anticonvulsants, antihypertensives, insulin, anticoagulants, antipsychotics for stable schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, mood stabilizers, antidepressants, and asthma or COPD medications are restarted as soon as the provider has an order based on the best verified information available.

Self-report Start here

Name, strength, frequency, last dose, prescriber, pharmacy — captured from the patient.

PDMP + EHR Verify controlled

Check the state PDMP for all controlled substances (CDC 2022 — every admission); check Lightning Step for prior-fill history in our system.

Pharmacy + prescriber Confirm

Call the home pharmacy (document pharmacist, date/time); call the prescriber when verification is incomplete or input is needed.

Provider order Restart

Communicate the verified list to the admitting provider, who orders the restart. No medication without an active order — but don't wait to restart essentials.

Restart by Class · The Details That Differ
Narration · Same Time-Based Frame, Class-Specific Twists

The time-since-last-dose framework — last effective dose under two weeks, about half at two-to-four weeks, standard initial dose at four-to-six weeks, and a full new start beyond six weeks — applies across the psychiatric classes, but each class has a twist worth knowing. Among SSRIs and SNRIs, paroxetine and the short-half-life SNRIs like venlafaxine immediate-release produce discontinuation symptoms within days, so even a three-to-seven-day lapse warrants prompt restart at the last effective dose; fluoxetine, by contrast, has such a long half-life that it tolerates longer gaps without adjustment. Bupropion should be re-titrated because its seizure risk is dose-dependent. Among antipsychotics, the clozapine rule is absolute: more than forty-eight hours off, and you must re-titrate from 12.5 milligrams, with ANC monitoring under the REMS program. Among mood stabilizers, lithium needs renal function and TSH checked and levels followed; and lamotrigine carries its own non-negotiable rule — more than about five days off, re-titrate from 25 milligrams a day because of the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, even after just a one-to-two-week lapse. ADHD stimulants are held during acute detox and need PDMP verification. And MAOIs and tricyclics require direct psychiatric input — with a washout of fourteen days, or five weeks for fluoxetine, when switching between an MAOI and a serotonergic agent, to prevent serotonin syndrome.

ClassThe Class-Specific Rule
SSRIs / SNRIsTime-based frame; paroxetine & short-half-life SNRIs → restart even after 3–7 day lapse; fluoxetine tolerates long gaps
Bupropion / tetracyclicsRe-titrate bupropion (dose-dependent seizure risk); mirtazapine/trazodone per time frame
Clozapine> 48 h off → re-titrate from 12.5 mg; ANC monitoring (REMS); call DON & VPMA
Other antipsychoticsRestart at last effective dose if < 2 wk; monitor orthostasis & sedation; metabolic monitoring
LithiumVerify renal function & TSH; follow serum levels (0.8–1.2 mEq/L); titrate after longer gaps
Valproate / carbamazepineSerum-level monitoring; watch carbamazepine autoinduction on restart; LFTs with alcohol history
Lamotrigine> ~5 days off → re-titrate from 25 mg/day (Stevens-Johnson risk) — even after a 7–14 day lapse
ADHD stimulantsDo not restart in acute detox (Days 1–7); PDMP verification; individualized if stimulant use disorder
MAOIs / TCAsDirect psychiatric input; washout 14 days (5 weeks for fluoxetine) when switching with serotonergic agents

Why discontinuation gets mistaken for relapse

Abruptly stopping a short-half-life antidepressant produces a discontinuation syndrome — the FINISH cluster: flu-like symptoms, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory disturbance, and hyperarousal. On a detox unit it's easy to read those as relapse, new withdrawal, or new psychiatric pathology, which sends the plan of care sideways. Recognizing it as discontinuation — and restarting promptly — is often the whole fix.

When symptoms appear within days of an antidepressant lapse, think discontinuation syndrome first, not new diagnosis.

Agents That Need Extra Care
Class-by-Class Restart Guidance
SSRIs / SNRIs
Sertraline, fluoxetine, venlafaxine, duloxetine. Prior dose if the gap is under 4 weeks; 50% and titrate if 4–8 weeks or unclear. Full therapeutic effect takes 4–6 weeks — don't adjust for efficacy in the first two weeks unless adverse effects emerge. Discontinuation syndrome is possible after gaps over 2 weeks: dizziness, nausea, flu-like symptoms, electric-shock sensations.
Bupropion
Lowers the seizure threshold — hold until at least Day 5–7 of stable detox, especially with alcohol or benzodiazepines.
Quetiapine
Commonly prescribed for sleep or anxiety in SUD settings — restart at the lowest effective prior dose, clarify and document the original indication, and watch for EPS in early recovery.
Mood stabilizers
Lithium needs serum-level verification within 5–7 days (narrow index, 0.8–1.2 mEq/L) plus renal assessment with significant alcohol history. Valproate needs LFTs with significant alcohol use. Carbamazepine needs CBC and LFTs and has multiple interactions.
Antipsychotics (atypicals)
Restart at the lowest effective prior dose and titrate as tolerated; metabolic monitoring — weight, glucose, lipids — is recommended. Clozapine requires ANC monitoring and REMS registration; consult psychiatry before restart.
Benzodiazepines
Contraindicated in SUD settings without direct psychiatric oversight and documented justification — managed only within the detox protocol framework. Avoid new prescribing without formal psychiatric consultation and a documented risk-benefit analysis.
Stimulants (ADHD)
Do not restart during acute detox, Days 1–7.
Restart, Monitor — and Time the Assessment
Narration · The Brain Re-Regulates Over Weeks

Here's the principle that ties psychiatric care together: the NP restarts all clinically appropriate psychiatric medications and monitors the response — but the brain re-regulates over weeks, and withdrawal can mimic psychiatric illness, so timing the formal evaluation matters as much as the restart itself. Understanding the neurobiology helps. In the first few days, you have GABA-glutamate imbalance, noradrenergic hyperactivity, dopamine depletion, and a cortisol surge — so anxiety, dysphoria, agitation, even hallucinations are largely withdrawal-mediated. As the days pass, the HPA axis slowly settles, sleep architecture begins to recover, and dopamine and serotonin systems partially restore. That's why there's a window — roughly twenty to thirty days sober — where a psychiatric assessment is finally reliable. One rule overrides the entire timeline, though: any imminent safety risk is escalated immediately, regardless of the day, and any documented pre-existing psychiatric disorder is treated as real from the start.

Days 1–3 Acute withdrawal

Symptoms reflect withdrawal, not a stable baseline — GABA-glutamate imbalance, noradrenergic surge, cortisol spike. Do not diagnose new psychiatric illness now. Restart all safe and appropriate psychiatric medications. Exception: imminent safety risk or documented pre-existing disorder.

Days 4–10 Early recovery

The key differentiation window. Autonomic symptoms settle; mood and sleep still fluctuate. Withdrawal-driven mood symptoms should begin improving — persistent or worsening symptoms after Day 5 warrant screening with C-SSRS, PHQ-9, and HAM-A. Keep restarting home meds and monitoring.

Days 10–20 Stabilizing / PAWS

Neurochemistry re-regulating; post-acute withdrawal symptoms (PAWS) may appear — cognitive fog, anhedonia, insomnia, cravings. Mood, anxiety, and ADHD become more evaluable. PHQ-9 scores are now clinically meaningful; titration can begin.

Days 20–30 Most reliable window

The most accurate point in this episode for psychiatric assessment and a psychiatric consult — roughly 20+ days sober. Antidepressants, mood stabilizers, and anxiolytics can be reliably evaluated and titrated; dual-diagnosis conceptualization is now possible; PTSD symptoms may surface as acute distress fades.

Interactive · Case Scenario

Day two, feeling hopeless

It's Day 2 of an alcohol detox. The patient is tearful and says, "I think I've always been depressed — I probably need a diagnosis and new medication." Her PHQ-9 today is 13, item 9 negative. She stopped her home sertraline about three weeks ago.

Question 1 — The right move today is:

Exactly — restart and monitor. A 2–4 week gap means roughly half the prior dose with titration, and acute withdrawal is not the moment to diagnose new psychiatric illness.
Think about the Days 1–3 window and the restart framework for a three-week gap. Try again.

Question 2 — When is the most reliable window for her formal psychiatric assessment?

Right — the 20–30 day window is the most accurate point for assessment, and safety always overrides the timeline.
The brain re-regulates over weeks — there's a specific window where assessment is most reliable. Try again.

When Psychiatry Can't Wait
Narration · Escalation Overrides the Clock

The twenty-to-thirty-day window is about accuracy, not about making a patient wait when they're in danger. Certain presentations are escalated the moment you see them, regardless of the day of detox. Active suicidal ideation with a plan or intent. Homicidal ideation. Psychosis that isn't explained by withdrawal. Mania. Catatonia. Severe agitation that doesn't respond to PRN medication. Decompensation in someone with a known serious mental illness. For those, you escalate now. And our screening tools carry their own action thresholds — let's walk through them, because these numbers trigger specific responses.

Screen & ScoreRequired Action

PHQ-9 15–19Moderately severe → consult required
PHQ-9 20–27Severe → URGENT consult
PHQ-9 item 9 positiveComplete C-SSRS, notify provider, continuous monitoring
C-SSRS L2Active SI → psych consult
C-SSRS L3SI with method, no plan → urgent consult + Q15 monitoring
C-SSRS L4SI with some intent → 1:1 sitter, means restriction, transfer eval
C-SSRS L5SI with plan & intent → immediate consult, continuous 1:1, transfer
GAD-7 15–21Severe → psych consult
Any suicidal behavior, past 3 moImmediate consult + 1:1

VII.

Special Populations & MAT

Nurse practitioner & medical team focus · ≈35 minutes
Listen to this chapter. Checking for recorded narration…
Narration · When the Protocol Steps Aside

Most patients are managed with the duration-driven protocols from Chapter Five. But some patients need the protocol set aside entirely in favor of an individualized plan, and pregnancy is the clearest example. There are no standing-order detox protocols for pregnant patients — every order is individualized after provider evaluation, and the Medical Director is notified immediately on any positive test or report. This is why a pregnancy test is part of every female-born admission, before any protocol starts. For opioid use disorder in pregnancy, maintenance is preferred over withdrawal, because maintenance minimizes precipitated withdrawal and unnecessary fetal naloxone exposure. Subutex — the monoproduct, without naloxone — is standard, and methadone is offered at Millbury and Philadelphia. The principle to carry: in pregnancy, you slow down, you escalate to the Medical Director, and you individualize.

Pregnancy & Diabetes
Pregnancy in Substance Use Disorder
Notify immediately
Any positive pregnancy test or report → notify the Medical Director immediately. This is non-negotiable and time-sensitive.
No standing orders
There are no standing-order detox protocols for pregnant patients — orders are individualized after provider evaluation.
OUD approach
Maintenance is preferred over withdrawal; Subutex (the monoproduct) is standard, minimizing precipitated withdrawal and fetal naloxone exposure. Methadone is offered at Millbury and Philadelphia.
Screening
Pregnancy testing is part of every female-born admission — it precedes protocol selection, not the other way around.
Diabetic Patients — Correction-Dose (Sliding Scale) Insulin
Monitoring
Capillary blood glucose on admission; checks QAC, QHS, and PRN. Target range 100–180 mg/dL. Sliding insulin is a short-term measure.

Naltrexone for AUD · The Protocol in Depth
Narration · Day 3, and the LFT Myth

The naltrexone protocol exists because of one hard fact: detoxification alone is not adequate treatment for alcohol use disorder. Without relapse-prevention pharmacotherapy, post-detox relapse rates run sixty to eighty percent within ninety days, concentrated in the first two weeks after discharge — exactly when the patient re-enters their triggers. So naltrexone fifty milligrams by mouth daily starts on Day 3 of the inpatient stay, while the benzodiazepine taper is still active, because there's no interaction — the FDA label even lists benzodiazepines as a preferred pain option in patients on naltrexone. Starting inpatient, not at discharge, is the point: it builds therapeutic levels, confirms tolerability, and completes education before the patient leaves, which is what actually drives outpatient adherence. The single most important safety check is opioid status: naltrexone is absolutely contraindicated with any current opioid use or agonist treatment, so confirm the patient has been opioid-free seven to ten days — ten to fourteen if they were on methadone or buprenorphine — because precipitated withdrawal is a medical emergency. And here's the myth to unlearn: baseline liver function tests are not required before starting. The FDA removed naltrexone's hepatotoxicity black-box warning after trials showed enzyme elevations at the same rate as placebo; the true hepatic contraindication is acute hepatitis or fulminant liver failure, not elevated enzymes, and even compensated cirrhosis is not a contraindication. A 25-milligram titration for three days is an option for anticipated GI sensitivity, but the Day 3 start holds.

Naltrexone — Order, Contraindications & Education
Standing order
Naltrexone (ReVia) 50 mg PO daily, starting Day 3, each day until discharge; concurrent with the benzo taper. Optional 25 mg × 3 days for GI sensitivity. Provider signs after the contraindication checklist.
Absolute contraindications
Any current opioid use or positive opioid UDS; methadone or buprenorphine MAT; active opioid detox; not opioid-free 7–10 days (10–14 if methadone/bup); acute hepatitis; fulminant hepatic failure; hypersensitivity; or any signs of opioid withdrawal.
LFT policy
Baseline LFTs not required; never delay initiation awaiting results. Order LFTs as part of the admission panel and manage by the decision framework. Discontinue only for AST/ALT > 10× ULN with symptoms.
Critical education
Naltrexone blocks all opioids — never try to override the blockade (life-threatening). Carry a medication ID card; tell every provider before any pain medication or procedure. Not an opioid, not euphoric, not habit-forming; abstinence not required to start.
Monitoring
Baseline vitals/symptoms before and 2 h after the first dose; daily inquiry for nausea, GI symptoms, mood, and opioid-withdrawal-like symptoms (tearfulness, myalgia, rhinorrhea) — if those appear, assess for occult opioid use and obtain a UDS.
Discharge
30-day supply, 0 refills (outpatient provider continues); follow-up in 7–14 days, monthly up to 12 months; consider Vivitrol 380 mg IM monthly for adherence. Alternatives if not tolerated: acamprosate (liver-safe, renally cleared), gabapentin, disulfiram.

Benzodiazepines and naltrexone — safe together

A common hesitation is whether naltrexone can run alongside the alcohol-withdrawal benzo taper. It can. Benzodiazepines have no pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interaction with naltrexone, and the FDA label actually names benzodiazepines as a preferred pain option for patients on naltrexone. Gabapentin is also a beneficial combination — an RCT found naltrexone plus gabapentin lengthened the time to heavy drinking versus naltrexone alone, especially with poor sleep.

"Wait until the taper is done" is not a reason to delay naltrexone. Day 3, concurrent, is the protocol.

Spravato (Esketamine) · The Full Protocol
Narration · A Different Mechanism, a Structured Session

Spravato — esketamine — is an intranasal medication for treatment-resistant depression and for major depressive disorder with acute suicidal ideation or behavior, offered through Affinity One and The Counseling Center under the FDA-mandated REMS program. It works differently from every antidepressant we've discussed: it's an NMDA-receptor antagonist that boosts glutamate, activates AMPA receptors, and drives synaptogenesis, which is why its effects can appear within hours rather than weeks. Treatment-resistant depression here means an inadequate response to at least two oral antidepressants of adequate dose and duration in the current episode. The session is structured and supervised: complete a PHQ-9 before dosing; confirm the patient hasn't taken benzodiazepines, psychostimulants, non-benzodiazepine sedatives, or MAOIs; take a baseline blood pressure; administer the nasal sprays five minutes apart — 56 milligrams, two sprays, for the first treatment, and 84 milligrams, three sprays, for subsequent doses; check blood pressure again at forty minutes; and a final check ten minutes before the two-hour mark, assessing for sedation and dissociation and confirming transportation. The schedule is twice weekly for the first month, weekly for the second, then weekly or every two weeks for maintenance. The two side effects to expect are dissociation — in sixty to eighty-four percent of patients — and a blood-pressure rise that peaks around forty minutes and lasts about four hours. And the firm rule: no driving or operating machinery until after a full night's rest.

Spravato — Essentials
Mechanism
NMDA-receptor antagonist → increased glutamate → AMPA activation → synaptogenesis; onset within hours, unlike monoaminergic antidepressants.
Indications
Treatment-resistant depression (failed ≥ 2 adequate oral antidepressants this episode); MDD with acute suicidal ideation/behavior (no prior trial required).
Contraindications
Uncontrolled hypertension; history of stroke or brain bleed; aneurysm/AVM; esketamine sensitivity.
The session
PHQ-9 first; screen for benzos/stimulants/sedatives/MAOIs; BP at baseline, 40 min, and pre-discharge; dosing 56 mg (2 sprays) initial, 84 mg (3 sprays) thereafter, 5 min apart; ~2-hour observation.
Schedule
Weeks 1–4 twice weekly; weeks 5–8 weekly; week 9+ weekly or every 2 weeks. NP follow-up between stages.
Side effects & rule
Dissociation (61–84%), transient BP rise (peak ~40 min, ~4 h), sedation, nausea, mild headache. No driving or machinery until after a full night's rest. No heavy meal for 2 h before.

Relapse Prevention & Medication-Assisted Treatment
Narration · Naltrexone for Alcohol Use Disorder

Naltrexone deserves its own moment, because the evidence is strong and the timing is specific. The principle behind the protocol is that detoxification alone is not adequate treatment for alcohol use disorder — without relapse-prevention pharmacotherapy, most patients return to heavy drinking within days to weeks, and the highest risk is the first two weeks after discharge. So naltrexone, fifty milligrams by mouth daily, is started on Day 3 of the inpatient stay, concurrent with the benzodiazepine taper — and there's no interaction between the two; the FDA label even lists benzodiazepines as a preferred option in patients on naltrexone. The single most important safety point: naltrexone is absolutely contraindicated with any current opioid use or opioid agonist treatment, so we confirm the patient has been opioid-free for seven to ten days — ten to fourteen if they were on methadone or buprenorphine. We educate thoroughly, especially that naltrexone blocks all opioids and they must never try to override it. We monitor GI side effects and liver symptoms — and notably, baseline liver function tests are not required before initiation. And because the protection only works if it continues, the patient leaves with a prescription and outpatient follow-up.

Naltrexone — Inpatient Protocol for AUD
Day 3 start
Naltrexone 50 mg PO daily begins Day 3, concurrent with the benzo taper — no interaction.
Opioid-free first
Absolute contraindication with any opioid use or MAT. Confirm opioid-free 7–10 days; 10–14 if methadone or buprenorphine.
Educate & monitor
Opioid-blockade safety (never override it), GI side effects, liver symptoms. No mandatory pre-treatment LFTs.
Continue at discharge
Discharge prescription plus outpatient follow-up — relapse protection only works if it continues.
Narration · MAT / MOUD Across the Continuum

Medication-assisted treatment — medication for opioid use disorder — is among the most effective things we do. Buprenorphine and methadone are first-line and life-saving: they reduce overdose mortality and all-cause mortality and keep patients in care, and they're offered across our continuum — Sunrise Detox, Evolve, Affinity One, and The Counseling Center. An important point on dosing: there is no single fixed dose. Dosing is individualized and follows ASAM guidelines and clinical criteria, and the patient's assessment data — COWS scores, history — informs the orders the provider writes. Reaching the final stable dose is a team decision: the NP works with the discharge-planning team and the patient to confirm a stable, effective dose before discharge. It is never a unilateral call. We also have long-acting options — Vivitrol, which is extended-release naltrexone, and Sublocade — that support adherence, with the same contraindications applying. And one more service to know by name: Spravato, offered through Affinity One and The Counseling Center, which requires a two-hour post-dose observation, with no driving or operating machinery until after a full night's rest. The bottom line: patients with opioid use disorder should be offered continued maintenance medication at discharge, not detox alone.

MAT / MOUD — The Essentials
First-line, life-saving
Buprenorphine and methadone reduce overdose and all-cause mortality and retain patients in care — offered across SDC, ERC, Affinity One, and TCC.
Dosing is individualized
No one-size dose; dosing follows ASAM guidelines and clinical criteria, informed by COWS scores and history.
A team decision at discharge
The NP works with the discharge-planning team and the patient to confirm a final stable dose — never unilateral. Offer continued maintenance MOUD at discharge, not detox alone.
Long-acting options
Vivitrol (extended-release naltrexone) and Sublocade support adherence; same contraindications apply.
Spravato
Affinity One and TCC. Two-hour post-dose observation; no driving or machinery until after a full night's rest.
