VIII.

Communication, Transitions & On-Call

For every team member · with NP-specific coverage rules · ≈35–40 minutes
Listen to this chapter. Checking for recorded narration…
Narration · One Team, Every Loop Closed

Communication is how a group of individuals becomes a team — and transitions and handoffs are exactly where care is most likely to break down, so that's where our communication has to be strongest. Microsoft Teams is our primary channel: use the right channels for clinical, operational, and leadership topics, tag messages with the correct urgency, and meet the response-time expectations set during onboarding. Although this is medical-team work, you never work alone — the medical team is one part of a larger multidisciplinary team, and decisions about the plan of care are coordinated together. Consults route through that team. You'll join the MDT meeting Monday through Friday, and whenever you're physically in the building, presenting your updates, labs, medication changes, and discharge plans. And every single day, you close the lab loop: the NP reviews and signs results daily, helps with the draw when nursing can't get it, and the DON backstops each morning. No dangling results — every result gets an owner and a follow-up.

The Wider Team
One Multidisciplinary Team — Who Coordinates the Plan
Counselors / Therapists
Lead clinical sessions, build treatment plans, drive engagement and aftercare.
Case Managers
Coordinate FMLA, disability, legal, housing, and benefits, including coordination of benefits.
Nursing
Continuous monitoring, the med pass, labs — your closest day-to-day partner.
Utilization Review
Secures authorizations so the level of care matches clinical need — your thorough ASAM-dimension documentation from Chapter Four directly supports their work.
Medical Providers
NP/APN and consultants — orders, MAT, and medical oversight. Consults route through the MDT.
Executive Director
Leads facility operations and the environment of care — the operational backbone that lets the clinical team focus on patients.
Closing the Loop, Every Shift

During the shift Teams

Use the correct clinical / operational / leadership channel; tag urgency; meet response-time expectations. Route consults through the MDT.

Daily Labs

The NP reviews and signs results every day and helps with the draw when nursing can't get it. The DON backstops each morning so nothing slips.

End of shift Summary

Post an end-of-shift summary to the Teams clinical group so the whole team is updated and every loop is closed with follow-up.

Before you leave In person

Check out in person with nursing and the DON. A clean verbal handoff on top of the written summary protects the next shift — and the patient.

Transitions of Care
Narration · Discharge Is Planned From Day One

Discharge isn't an event at the end — it's a plan that starts at admission. Aftercare planning begins on Day 1, and the whole stay points toward a safe transition. Counseling guides the destination: where the patient goes next, and where post-discharge medications and pharmacy should be set up. The provider confirms medical clearance — that the patient is medically stable for the next level of care — and that's a team decision, never unilateral. Then comes the warm handoff: records, prescriptions, and follow-up appointments arranged so the receiving team is ready. For opioid use disorder, maintenance medication continuity is arranged and naloxone is provided. One number worth remembering: continuing-care contact within seven days of discharge is associated with significantly reduced thirty-day rehospitalization — so the warm handoff isn't a courtesy, it's a clinical intervention.

Narration · Discharge Prescriptions & the Refill Rule

Discharge prescriptions follow a clear rule. First, the timing: scripts are written one to three days before discharge, not at the last minute, and verified against the PDMP. Then the refill count depends entirely on where the patient is going. If the patient is continuing within a Praesum program — Sunrise Detox, Evolve, Affinity One, or The Counseling Center — they receive a thirty-day supply plus one refill, because continuity of prescribing is assured within our own system. If the patient is going home or to a provider outside the Praesum system, they receive a thirty-day supply with zero refills, because the receiving provider assumes prescribing and we don't want orphaned controlled-substance refills floating outside a managing relationship. Regardless of destination, you always do the same five things: verify the discharge medication list, check the PDMP for controlled substances, ensure maintenance medication continuity for opioid use disorder, provide naloxone for any patient with OUD, and confirm the patient understands each medication. Match the prescription to who will be managing it next.

Where the Patient Is GoingDischarge Prescription
Continuing in a Praesum program30-day supply + 1 refill — continuity assured in our system
Home or a non-Praesum provider30-day supply + 0 refills — receiving provider assumes prescribing
Always — every dischargeVerify med list · check PDMP · MOUD continuity · naloxone for OUD · confirm patient understanding
Emergency-Contact Communication · The Daily Discipline
Narration · The Call That Reassures a Family

Emergency-contact communication is one of the most human parts of the job, and it has rules. EC contact is made daily for patients with a full release of information, and it's expected in the morning for new admissions — because a patient may not have made a safe call home, and the family needs to know they're with us and safe. If you say you'll follow up later in the day, you follow up; if the contact gives a best time to reach them, that goes in the note. Important information relayed gets documented in the contact note — and the working rule is the same one that governs all our documentation: if the outreach isn't in the chart, it didn't happen. Always ask whether there's anything the team should know and whether the contact has questions, and always relay that appropriate aftercare from detox is residential or PHP with sober living. For a Presence-In-Treatment contact — emergency-only — you can confirm the patient is here and will let them know at discharge, but nothing more; though the contact may share information with you. And the moment EC communication matters most is at discharge: nothing is worse than a family we've been talking with not knowing their loved one has been discharged or where they went.

EC Communication & Coordination of Benefits
Daily EC contact
Daily with full ROI; morning for new admissions. Document in the Contacts tab and the progress note; document attempted calls and voicemails too — don't wait to see if they call back.
Check the ROI first
Double-check releases before any call. For a Presence-In-Treatment (emergency-only) contact: confirm presence and discharge notification only; they may share with you, but you may not share clinical detail.
In-session vs. standalone
A call with just you is a contact note. A call with the patient in session is noted in the session note plus a separate contact note for the call.
Coordination of Benefits
Call Provider Services on the insurance card; verify this is the patient's only coverage; capture primary/secondary, reference number, and rep name. After 15 minutes on hold = one attempt; after 3 failed attempts, document the attempts.
Discharge · Plan vs. Summary
Narration · Two Documents, One Safe Transition

In Lightning Step there are two distinct discharge deliverables, and it's worth knowing which is which. The Discharge Plan is forward-looking, completed before discharge: it pulls from the treatment plan, documents the condition at discharge, the discharge type, the anticipated post-discharge plan, the medication list from nursing, and the anticipated effect of family dynamics, plus referrals. The Discharge Summary is retrospective — the record of the episode of care: admit and discharge dates, discharge type and code, funding source, the precipitating event with the admission quote, services provided, the medication list, the summary of treatment, the condition at discharge, and the continuing-care plan with specific dates and times. Both exist because a safe transition needs both a plan for what comes next and an accurate account of what happened. And whichever you're writing, the constants hold: verify the medication list, confirm MOUD continuity and naloxone for any opioid-use-disorder patient, and aim for continuing-care contact within seven days, which significantly reduces thirty-day rehospitalization.

Administrative Discharge · A High-Risk Transition
Narration · When a Patient Must Leave Early

Administrative discharge is the involuntary discharge of a patient before clinical completion — and it is one of the highest-risk transitions we manage, because leaving treatment early sharply elevates short-term overdose mortality. So it has guardrails. It's reserved for genuinely unmanageable situations: contraband or weapons on the unit despite intervention, physical aggression toward a patient or staff member, repeated willful rule violations after corrective attempts, or persistent unwillingness to engage after structured efforts. It is never a punishment for ambivalence, slow progress, or the very symptoms that brought the patient in — craving, withdrawal-related irritability. Before any administrative discharge: a multidisciplinary review including the DON, the on-call medical provider, and clinical leadership, with notification of the VP of Medical Affairs; documented evidence that less-restrictive interventions were tried; and a current medical and psychiatric assessment within the prior four hours, including vitals, the withdrawal scale, PHQ-9, and C-SSRS. A patient in active crisis — suicidal with a positive item 9 or C-SSRS Level 4 to 5, psychotic, in severe withdrawal, or unstable — is never discharged administratively; they're transferred to a higher level of care. And on the way out, harm reduction is mandatory: naloxone for every opioid-use-disorder patient, MOUD continuity with a warm handoff, written instructions with the 988 Lifeline and the SAMHSA helpline, safe transportation, and full documentation.

Administrative Discharge — Guardrails
Indications
Contraband/weapons despite intervention; physical aggression; repeated willful rule violations after correction; persistent refusal to engage after structured attempts.
Never for
Treatment ambivalence, slow progress, or symptoms that are themselves the indication for care (craving, withdrawal-related irritability).
Before discharge
MDT review (DON + on-call provider + clinical leadership), VPMA notified; documented less-restrictive attempts; medical/psychiatric assessment within 4 h (vitals, withdrawal scale, PHQ-9, C-SSRS); provider order.
Never discharge in crisis
Active SI (item 9 / C-SSRS L4–5), psychosis, severe withdrawal, or unstable vitals → transfer to higher level of care, not administrative discharge.
Harm reduction on exit
Naloxone for every OUD patient; MOUD continuity + warm handoff; written instructions with 988 and SAMHSA 1-800-662-HELP; ≥ 1 outpatient referral; safe transportation confirmed.

The behavior might be the illness

The reason administrative discharge requires a multidisciplinary review is that disruptive behavior is sometimes untreated medical or psychiatric pathology rather than willful disruption — agitation from withdrawal, irritability from a brewing delirium, impulsivity from an unmanaged psychiatric condition. The review exists to catch exactly that before a patient is sent into the highest-risk window of their care.

Before "this patient won't comply," ask "is this behavior a symptom we haven't treated yet?"

After Hours · On-Call
Narration · The Rules Tighten After Dark

On-call is how we keep coverage continuous after hours. The on-call period runs twenty-four hours, from seven in the morning to seven the next morning — or, when you arrive for a shift, from the time you enter the facility until seven the following morning. All nurse practitioners, including per diem providers, may carry the on-call phone, so you need to be ready: understand the expectations and the escalation criteria before your first on-call shift, and when you're unsure, escalate — the DON is your first contact. A rule we've emphasized all the way through applies especially after hours: do not change established detox protocols without team communication. After hours, your job is to stabilize the patient, document clearly, and escalate — not to rewrite the plan of care alone. And on-call is a personal responsibility: if you're scheduled and can't make a shift, you are responsible for arranging appropriate coverage and notifying the team. Coverage gaps are patient-safety gaps.

On-Call — Four Things to Internalize
24-hour coverage
7 AM to 7 AM the next day — or from when you enter the facility until 7 AM. All NPs, including per diem, may carry the phone.
Know your scope & criteria
Understand expectations and escalation criteria before your first shift. When unsure, escalate — the DON is first.
Don't change protocols solo
Do not change established detox protocols after hours without team communication. Stabilize, document, escalate.
Arrange your own coverage
If you're scheduled and can't make a shift, you arrange appropriate coverage and notify the team. Coverage gaps are patient-safety gaps.

A 2 AM call — symptoms breaking through the taper

Nursing calls: a patient's withdrawal symptoms are breaking through the established taper. The on-call NP's job isn't to rewrite the protocol from home — it's to stabilize with PRN comfort measures per protocol, document the assessment and the objective data clearly, and escalate, flagging the detox-medication concern for the DON and Main NP to address with the full team in daylight. Doing nothing isn't stabilizing; rewriting the taper alone isn't allowed. The middle path — stabilize, document, escalate — is the whole job after hours.

After hours, "stabilize, document, escalate" is not a fallback — it is the standard of care.

IX.

Going the Extra Mile

For every member of the patient care team · ≈30 minutes
Listen to this chapter. Checking for recorded narration…
Narration · Care Is How We Treat People

Patient-centered care isn't a slogan — it's how we deliver treatment, and it's what patients remember most. Lead with safety, build trust, and offer choice. Use person-first, respectful language, and ask permission before sensitive questions — "If you feel comfortable…". Honor each patient's preferences and goals; remember Dimension Six from Chapter Three — we build the plan with the patient, not simply for them. With a signed release of information, involving family and the emergency contact is associated with better retention and treatment completion. Our patients tell us what matters: a relaxed atmosphere with genuine caring between members, a counselor who's relatable, a judgment-free zone where they can express themselves. That's the bar. And one more thing that's easy to forget: your colleagues are your customers too. Going the extra mile means warm handoffs, answering the call you could have let ring, and closing loops nobody asked you to close — for patients, for families, and for the teammate picking up the next shift.

The Boundary That Keeps Us Consistent
Narration · Never Commit on the Spot

How we talk with clients is part of the treatment, and there's a clear boundary that keeps the whole team consistent. Be warm, transparent, and trauma-informed — and never commit on the spot to decisions that belong to the team. There are four things you don't commit to directly: discharge dates or early discharge; medical clearance to leave or return to work; completing forms like FMLA, disability, or court paperwork; and writing letters for employers, courts, or family. The reason isn't bureaucracy — it's that an individual promise made in a hallway becomes the team's problem and the patient's disappointment when it can't be kept. The move every time is the same: acknowledge warmly, tell them you'll bring it to the team, and close the loop with them once the team has decided. It's a customer-service principle that's also a safety principle.

Never Commit on the Spot — These Belong to the Team
Discharge
Discharge dates or early discharge — always the Main NP plus the full MDT, with confirmation the patient is stable and ready.
Medical clearance
Clearance to leave or to return to work.
Forms
Completing FMLA, disability, or court paperwork.
Letters
Writing letters for employers, courts, or family.
The script instead
Acknowledge warmly → "That's important — let me bring it to the team so we get it right" → bring it to the team → close the loop with the patient.
Interactive · Case Scenario

Saturday afternoon

It's Saturday afternoon. A patient who seems stable approaches you directly: "Can I be discharged early — today? I feel great, and my ride is already on the way."

Question 1 — What's the best response?

Exactly. Warm acknowledgment, bring it to the team, no on-the-spot commitment. Dismissing damages trust; over-promising sets the patient up for disappointment. Notice how this one moment pulls together all three pillars.
Think about "never commit on the spot" — and who actually makes discharge decisions. Try again.

Question 2 — Why can't you simply say yes, even if the patient looks ready?

Right — bringing it to the team protects the patient, the team's consistency, and you.
Look back at the discharge rule from Chapter Two — it applies here too. Try again.
